source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 2 (Rice-growing environment), by Preap Visarto, section 2.2 (Temperature). No elibrary URL visible.
text: Temperature affects rice at every growth stage, with different sensitivities by stage and by subspecies (indica vs. japonica). Germination: indica-type rice germinates normally at temperatures of about 13 degrees C and above (Oka, 1999); japonica-type rice can tolerate slightly lower germination temperatures than indica. Vegetative growth/tillering: the normal range for good tillering is roughly 25-30 degrees C; tillering rate drops outside this range. Reproductive stage (panicle formation and flowering) is the most temperature-sensitive period of the entire crop cycle. The critical window is short - within about 2-4 days of panicle initiation, and again around 20-30 days before heading during microsporogenesis (pollen mother cell formation/meiosis). The ideal temperature range for both indica and japonica during the reproductive stage is about 27-29 degrees C. If temperature drops too low during microsporogenesis, or if extreme heat occurs during the few hours of flowering/anthesis, pollen sterility results, directly reducing grain set - this damage can occur within hours of an extreme temperature event during flowering. Soil surface and root-zone temperature also matters: typical soil surface temperature for lowland rice fields is about 32-34 degrees C, versus about 30-32 degrees C for upland conditions; rice seedlings can tolerate soil surface temperatures up to roughly 40 degrees C at establishment, but temperatures above about 50 degrees C damage young seedlings. Root growth is most active below about 25 degrees C soil temperature and slows as soil temperature rises above that. Japonica varieties are noted as having a lower critical low-temperature threshold for flowering (around 13-14 degrees C) than indica, which is part of why japonica types are better suited to cooler, higher-altitude, or temperate rice-growing regions while indica dominates Cambodia's tropical lowlands.
